title: HTML structure and semantic elements
intro: HTML gives a web page its structure and meaning; CSS will later control how that structure looks. In this lesson, you will learn the basic HTML document structure and how semantic elements make pages easier for people, browsers, search engines, and assistive technologies to understand.
body:
## What is HTML? **HTML** stands for HyperText Markup Language. It is the standard markup language used to describe the structure of web documents. HTML is not primarily responsible for making a page beautiful. That is one of the main jobs of CSS. Instead, HTML describes what the content means. For example: ~~~html

My Task Manager

Keep track of the things you need to do.

~~~ The browser can understand that the first piece is a main heading and the second is a paragraph. This distinction becomes important later. A good web page is not just a collection of things that happen to look correct. Its underlying structure should communicate what each piece of content represents. ## Elements, tags, and nesting An HTML **element** is a piece of the document with a particular meaning or purpose. ~~~diagram {"type": "tree", "title": "Nesting becomes a tree", "caption": "Every element sits inside exactly one parent. Browsers, screen readers and JavaScript all read your page as this tree.", "root": {"label": "", "children": [{"label": "", "children": [{"label": ""}, {"label": "<meta>"}]}, {"label": "<body>", "highlight": true, "children": [{"label": "<header>", "children": [{"label": "<nav>"}]}, {"label": "<main>", "highlight": true, "children": [{"label": "<h1>"}, {"label": "<article>"}]}, {"label": "<footer>"}]}]}} ~~~ For example: ~~~html <p>Hello, world!</p> ~~~ The `<p>` is the opening tag, `</p>` is the closing tag, and everything between them is the element's content. Some elements do not have closing tags. An image is commonly written as: ~~~html <img src="photo.jpg" alt="A mountain at sunset"> ~~~ HTML elements can be **nested**, meaning one element can be placed inside another. ~~~html <p>Read the <strong>important</strong> information.</p> ~~~ Here, the `strong` element is inside the paragraph. Nesting should make sense. When elements overlap incorrectly, browsers may have to repair the HTML, which can lead to confusing results. Think of HTML as a tree rather than a flat list of tags. ~~~text body ├── h1 ├── p └── ul ├── li ├── li └── li ~~~ This tree-like structure becomes important when you later work with JavaScript and the DOM. ## Attributes add information HTML elements can have **attributes**. Attributes provide additional information about an element or change how it behaves. For example: ~~~html <a href="https://example.com">Visit the site</a> ~~~ Here, `href` is an attribute containing the link destination. An image commonly has attributes such as: ~~~html <img src="logo.png" alt="Company logo"> ~~~ `src` tells the browser where the image comes from, while `alt` provides alternative text. Different elements support different attributes. Some attributes, such as `id` and `class`, are widely used, while others are specific to particular elements. ## The HTML document skeleton A normal HTML document starts with a basic structure. ~~~html <!doctype html> <html lang="en"> <head> <meta charset="UTF-8"> <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"> <title>My Website

Hello!

~~~ Let's look at each part. ### The doctype The first line is: ~~~html ~~~ It tells the browser that the document should be interpreted as modern HTML. You do not need to think of it as an HTML element. It is a declaration that belongs at the beginning of the document. ### The html element The `` element is the root of the document. The `lang` attribute identifies the primary language: ~~~html ~~~ For a Hungarian page, you would normally use: ~~~html ~~~ This information helps browsers and assistive technologies understand the language of the document. ### The head The `` contains information about the document that is generally not displayed as the page's main content. For example: ~~~html Task Manager ~~~ `charset="UTF-8"` specifies the character encoding used by the document. UTF-8 supports a very large range of characters, including Hungarian accented characters. The viewport meta element is important for responsive pages. It tells mobile browsers how to treat the page's viewport, which is the visible area of the page. The `` provides the document title. It can appear in the browser tab and is also useful for bookmarks and search engines. ### The body The `<body>` contains the document's visible page content. ~~~html <body> <h1>Task Manager</h1> <p>Organise your work.</p> </body> ~~~ Most of the HTML you write for the actual interface will eventually live inside the body. ## Headings create an outline HTML provides six heading levels: ~~~html <h1>Main title</h1> <h2>Section title</h2> <h3>Subsection title</h3> <h4>Smaller heading</h4> <h5>Smaller heading</h5> <h6>Smallest heading</h6> ~~~ The heading level communicates the structure of the content. It should not simply be chosen because one heading looks larger than another. A simple page might have: ~~~text h1: Task Manager h2: Today's tasks h3: Work h3: Personal h2: Completed tasks ~~~ For a straightforward page, having one main `h1` is a good rule. Under it, use `h2` for major sections and `h3` for subsections within those sections. Avoid skipping levels simply for visual reasons. If something should look smaller, CSS can change its appearance without changing its semantic heading level. ## Paragraphs and lists Use `<p>` for paragraphs of text. ~~~html <p>This application helps you organise your daily tasks.</p> ~~~ For an unordered list, use `<ul>` and `<li>`: ~~~html <ul> <li>Learn HTML</li> <li>Learn CSS</li> <li>Build a website</li> </ul> ~~~ For an ordered list, use `<ol>`: ~~~html <ol> <li>Create the project</li> <li>Write the HTML</li> <li>Test the page</li> </ol> ~~~ The list item `<li>` belongs inside either an ordered or unordered list. ## Links Links use the `<a>` element and its `href` attribute. An **absolute URL** contains the complete web address: ~~~html <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/">MDN</a> ~~~ A **relative URL** points to a resource relative to the current website: ~~~html <a href="/about.html">About</a> ~~~ Relative links are common when navigating within the same website. You can also link to another page relative to the current location: ~~~html <a href="contact.html">Contact</a> ~~~ To open a link in a new browsing context, you can use: ~~~html <a href="https://example.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">External site</a> ~~~ `target="_blank"` requests a new browsing context, commonly a new tab. When using it for an external link, `rel="noopener noreferrer"` is a useful security and privacy measure. Do not make every link open a new tab. Normal navigation generally works better when the user remains in the current tab. ## Images and meaningful alt text Images use the `<img>` element: ~~~html <img src="mountain.jpg" alt="Snow-covered mountain above a lake"> ~~~ The `alt` attribute provides alternative text for people who cannot see the image or when the image cannot be displayed. Good alt text describes the meaningful content of the image. Weak: ~~~html <img src="mountain.jpg" alt="image"> ~~~ Better: ~~~html <img src="mountain.jpg" alt="Snow-covered mountain above a lake"> ~~~ Do not stuff keywords into alt text for search engines. Write it for people who need the alternative description. If an image is purely decorative and adds no meaningful information, there are cases where an empty alt attribute is appropriate: ~~~html <img src="decoration.svg" alt=""> ~~~ The important lesson is that the `alt` attribute should be intentional, not forgotten. ## Semantic HTML One of the most important HTML habits is using elements according to their meaning. ~~~compare {"left": {"title": "div soup", "lang": "html", "code": "<div class=\"top\">\n <div class=\"links\">…</div>\n</div>\n<div class=\"content\">\n <div class=\"title\">Tasks</div>\n</div>", "note": "Works visually, but tells assistive technology nothing."}, "right": {"title": "Semantic HTML", "lang": "html", "code": "<header>\n <nav>…</nav>\n</header>\n<main>\n <h1>Tasks</h1>\n</main>", "note": "Same look with CSS — plus landmarks, an outline and better SEO."}} ~~~ HTML provides semantic elements such as: - `header` — introductory content for a page or section. - `nav` — a section containing navigation links. - `main` — the main content of the document. - `section` — a thematic section of content. - `article` — a self-contained piece of content. - `aside` — related content that is separate from the main flow. - `footer` — footer information for a page or section. These elements tell the browser and other software what the content represents. For example: ~~~html <header> <h1>My Blog</h1> <nav> <a href="/">Home</a> <a href="/articles">Articles</a> <a href="/about">About</a> </nav> </header> <main> <article> <h2>Learning HTML</h2> <p>HTML gives your content structure.</p> </article> </main> <footer> <p>© 2026 My Blog</p> </footer> ~~~ This is much more informative than putting everything inside generic containers. ## div and span still have a place You will also use `<div>` and `<span>`. A `<div>` is a generic block-level container. A `<span>` is a generic inline container. They do not communicate a specific semantic meaning by themselves. For example: ~~~html <div class="card"> <h2>Product</h2> <p>Description</p> </div> ~~~ There is nothing wrong with using a `div` when no more appropriate semantic element exists. The problem is using generic containers for everything: ~~~html <div class="header"> <div class="navigation"> <div class="main-content"> ... </div> </div> </div> ~~~ If those containers actually represent a header, navigation, and main content, semantic elements communicate that meaning much more clearly. Use `span` similarly when you need a generic inline container without a more appropriate semantic element. ## Why semantics matter Semantic HTML helps **accessibility**. Accessibility means designing websites so that people with different abilities and assistive technologies can use them effectively. Screen readers and other assistive technologies can use semantic structure to understand landmarks such as navigation and main content. Semantics also help search engines understand the structure and meaning of a page. This is one part of good **SEO** (Search Engine Optimisation). Search engines use many signals, so semantic HTML does not magically make a page rank highly. But clear structure makes your content easier for machines to interpret. Semantic HTML also helps developers. When you open a large document and see `header`, `nav`, `main`, and `article`, you can understand its structure more quickly than when everything is a `div`. ## A complete example page Here is a small but realistic HTML page that combines the concepts from this lesson. ~~~html <!doctype html> <html lang="en"> <head> <meta charset="UTF-8"> <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"> <title>Learn Web Development

Learn Web Development

Home Lessons About

HTML Basics

HTML gives web pages their structure and meaning.

  • Elements
  • Attributes
  • Semantic HTML

Next Steps

After HTML, you can learn how CSS controls presentation.

Learn CSS

© 2026 Learn Web Development

~~~ Notice how the structure tells a story even before CSS is added. There is one document, one main heading, navigation, main content with two thematic sections, an image with alternative text, and a footer. If you removed all the CSS, the page would not look polished, but its structure and meaning would still make sense. ## A practical way to think about HTML When creating a page, start by asking what each piece of content actually is. Is it the main heading? Use `h1`. Is it a paragraph? Use `p`. Is it navigation? Use `nav`. Is it the main content? Use `main`. Is it a thematic group of content? Consider `section`. Is it an independent article or post? Consider `article`. Is it related secondary information? Consider `aside`. Only after choosing the appropriate structure should you worry about how the elements look. CSS will let you make an `h2` look smaller, a `nav` horizontal, or a `section` look like a card. HTML's job is to describe what those things are. ## A short HTML checklist Before considering a basic HTML page finished, check: 1. Does the document have ``? 2. Does `` have the correct `lang` attribute? 3. Does the head contain UTF-8 character encoding and a viewport declaration? 4. Does the page have a useful ``? 5. Is there a clear heading structure? 6. Are links real `<a>` elements with meaningful `href` values? 7. Do images have appropriate `alt` text? 8. Are semantic elements used where they make sense? 9. Is there one clear `<main>` element? 10. Could another developer understand the page structure without seeing the CSS? Good HTML is not about using as many elements as possible. It is about choosing elements that accurately describe the content. Once you have that foundation, CSS and JavaScript can build on it without having to compensate for a confusing document structure.
takeaways: HTML describes the structure and meaning of content rather than its visual appearance.
Elements can contain other elements, while attributes provide additional information or behaviour.
A basic document needs a doctype, language declaration, head metadata, title, and body content.
Semantic elements such as header, nav, main, section, article, aside, and footer communicate meaning to browsers, assistive technologies, search engines, and developers.
Use div and span when you need generic containers, but prefer a meaningful semantic element when one accurately describes the content.

quiz.question: What is HTML primarily responsible for?
options: Defining the structure and meaning of web content
Choosing the colours of every element
quiz.explanation: HTML describes the structure and meaning of content. CSS is primarily responsible for presentation and visual styling.

quiz.question: Which element normally contains the main visible content of an HTML document?
quiz.explanation: The body contains the document's page content that is presented to the user.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the alt attribute on an image?
options: To make the image load faster
To provide alternative text describing the image's meaningful content
To specify the image's CSS width
To make the image open in a new tab
quiz.explanation: Alternative text helps people who cannot see the image and can also be used when the image cannot be displayed.

quiz.question: Which element is most appropriate for a page's primary navigation links?
quiz.explanation: The nav element represents a section containing navigation links.

quiz.question: Why is semantic HTML useful?
options: It eliminates the need for JavaScript.
It communicates document meaning and structure to users, tools, and assistive technologies.
It guarantees a page will rank first in search results.
quiz.explanation: Semantic HTML provides meaningful structure that can help accessibility, search engines, and developers understand the page. It does not guarantee a particular search ranking.

exercise.title: Rebuild a page with semantic HTML
exercise.task: Starting from the div-only page below, rebuild the document using semantic HTML elements while keeping the same basic content. The tests expect the root `html` element to have a `lang` attribute, exactly one `h1` inside a `header`, and a `nav` containing at least three links with `href` attributes. The `main` element must contain at least two `section` elements, each with an `h2`, every image must have non-empty `alt` text, and the `footer` must contain a `p` element. You may add or remove wrapper elements as needed, but produce a complete HTML document.

exercise.hint: Think about what each div represents rather than how it looks. The outer page areas map naturally to header, main, and footer; the navigation belongs in nav; the two content blocks are sections with h2 headings; and each image needs meaningful alt text.

tests.name: The page declares its language
tests.code: const html = document.documentElement; return html.hasAttribute('lang') && html.getAttribute('lang').trim() !== '';

tests.name: It has one main heading in the header
The main content has two titled sections
tests.code: const main = document.querySelector('main'); const sections = main ? main.querySelectorAll(':scope > section') : []; return sections.length >= 2 && Array.from(sections).every(section => !!section.querySelector('h2'));

tests.name: Images have alternative text and the footer has a paragraph
tests.code: const images = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('img')); const imagesValid = images.every(img => img.hasAttribute('alt') && img.getAttribute('alt').trim() !== ''); const footer = document.querySelector('footer'); return imagesValid && !!footer && !!footer.querySelector('p');
